title: The Ox of Sicily: Roccasecca to Fossanova, and the Bones to Toulouse
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Roccasecca, birth in the castle of the Conti di Aquino
stops.date_confidence: Year contested and not resolved here: New Advent gives 1225 or 1227, the Stanford Encyclopedia gives around 1225, critical scholarship c. 1224/25. No day or month survives; defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is the town center of Roccasecca, not the castle's own point, which no source consulted fixes.
stops.campa: A son is born to Landulf of Aquino, lord of Roccasecca, and to his wife Theodora. Landulf's youngest is meant for Monte Cassino, and through Monte Cassino for an abbacy: a great house, its revenues, and a nephew of the counts of Aquino holding both. The family are frontier nobility of the Kingdom of Sicily, they hold a pass between the emperor's country and the pope's, and they have the habit of placing sons where power is. The fortress they live in was raised by the abbots of Monte Cassino in 994 to close the Liri valley. Neither the day nor the year of the birth is fixed.
suggested_refs: The ruins of the Castello dei Conti di Aquino above Roccasecca, built by Monte Cassino in 994

stops.name: Monte Cassino, the child given to the abbey
stops.date_confidence: New Advent puts him at Monte Cassino from about age five; the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy dates the period c. 1229-1239, the Stanford Encyclopedia c. 1231-1239. Month and day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: At about five he is handed over as an oblate to the Benedictine abbey on the mountain, and the abbey takes him for what he is, a great family's donation with a career attached. He learns letters, chant, the psalter, and the Rule. Nine years pass that way, in a library on a mountain standing between an emperor's country and a pope's. The often-repeated story that the child pestered his masters with one question, what is God, belongs to the lives written for his canonization. No document made while he was there mentions him at all.
suggested_refs: The abbey library and scriptorium of Monte Cassino, destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly since

stops.name: Monte Cassino, the emperor's soldiers in the cloister
stops.date_confidence: R for the mechanism. The Wikipedia article on Montecassino attests only that Frederick II garrisoned troops in the abbey in 1239 during his war with the papacy, and does not mention Thomas at all; the standard biographical reconstruction that suspect monks were expelled and Thomas sent away in consequence is Torrell-line inference. Month unknown.
stops.campa: Frederick II, excommunicate and at war with Gregory IX, puts his soldiers inside the abbey. What follows for the oblate is not written down in any document made that year. The reconstruction that has come down holds that monks the emperor distrusted were turned out, and that Landulf's son went south with them to the emperor's own new university at Naples. Whether he was expelled, sent, or simply moved before the fighting reached the mountain, nothing surviving from 1239 says. The mountain school ends. He is fourteen.
suggested_refs: Frederick II's 1239 campaign against Gregory IX and the garrisoning of Montecassino

segments.name: Naples, the Habit, and the Tower

stops.name: Naples, the emperor's university
stops.date_confidence: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives the autumn of 1239 for the start of the Naples studies; the Stanford chronology gives c. 1239. Month set to September for the autumn term. Coordinate approximates the Nido district near San Marco, which Wikipedia says is only hypothesized as the medieval site.
stops.campa: Frederick II founded this studium in 1224 to make officials for his kingdom, outside church control, and its arts faculty teaches what Paris had spent thirty years forbidding. Here Thomas reads Aristotle whole: the logic first, then the physics and the metaphysics that came into Latin through Toledo and through the Arabic commentators, banned at Paris in 1210 and taught in Naples without apology. His masters are named as Peter of Ireland and a Master Martin. A Benedictine oblate is learning the Philosopher from an emperor's teachers, and of what either man taught him nothing survives in his own hand.
suggested_refs: The 1224 foundation charter of the studium of Naples
The Toledo translations of Aristotle and of the Arabic commentators

stops.name: Naples, San Domenico Maggiore: the habit taken
stops.date_confidence: Sources disagree and this is not resolved: the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives April 1244, New Advent puts the entry anywhere between 1240 and August 1243. Day unknown. Coordinate is the canonical atlas pin for San Domenico Maggiore.
stops.campa: The Order of Preachers is twenty-eight years old, mendicant, landless, and it recruits in the universities. Thomas takes its habit in the friary beside San Domenico Maggiore, and the family that placed him at Monte Cassino for an abbacy learns that its youngest has instead sworn to own nothing and to beg. His mother Theodora goes to Naples after him; the friars have already moved him north. Whether he chose the habit at nineteen or at seventeen the sources do not agree, and none of them records what he said to her.
suggested_refs: The Dominican friary of San Domenico Maggiore, Naples, where he received the habit and where he died to the world twice

stops.name: Acquapendente, taken off the road by his brothers
stops.date_confidence: New Advent gives the interception near Aquapendente in 1244 with no month; month set for ordering only. Coordinate corrected to the Wikipedia point for the comune of Acquapendente, 42.74389 / 11.86444; the exact place on the road is not preserved in any source consulted.
stops.campa: On the road north of the lake his brothers, soldiers in the emperor's service, take him off it. The Dominicans travelling with him are scattered or let go; the novice is put on a horse and carried back south into his own family's country. This is not an abduction by strangers. It is a household correcting a career decision by the means available to a household with armed sons, and it holds. New Advent, writing in 1913, says he was detained nearly two years; the Stanford chronology gives 1244 to 1245.
suggested_refs: The Via Cassia north of Bolsena, the Rome road the Dominicans were taking him along

stops.name: Monte San Giovanni Campano, the year in the fortress
stops.date_confidence: The detention is attested across sources; its length is not agreed, New Advent saying nearly two years and the Stanford chronology giving 1244-1245. Month arbitrary, for ordering. The temptation episode is canonization-era testimony repeated as fact by the Italian Wikipedia article on the castle, and is tagged R here.
stops.campa: They shut him in the Aquino fortress at Monte San Giovanni. What is attested is duller and heavier than what is told: a young man kept in a tower by his own family for the better part of a year, who argues with them and does not give way. The rest comes from testimony gathered for his canonization seventy years later and from no earlier record. In that account his brothers send a woman into the room to break his vow, and he drives her out with a brand snatched out of the fire and bars the door behind her.
sources: Wikipedia (Italian), 'Castello di Monte San Giovanni Campano'
suggested_refs: The canonization depositions of 1319 and 1321, source of the temptation story

stops.name: Roccasecca, the family gives way
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford chronology says his parents yielded and he went to Paris as a Dominican friar, dating the whole episode 1244-1245. The escape through a window and the winning-over of his sisters are New Advent's 1913 account and are tradition, not document. Month set for ordering.
stops.campa: The custody moves back to Roccasecca and then it ends. In the family's own telling, preserved by the Dominicans who wrote his life, his sisters were sent to argue him out of the order and were argued into it instead, and his mother let him down through a window rather than admit in public that the house had given way. The plainer reading is that a year of holding him produced nothing and the cost of continuing outran the point. He is let go in 1245 and goes to Paris, in the habit he was taken in.
suggested_refs: William of Tocco's Ystoria sancti Thomae de Aquino, source of the window and the sisters

stops.name: Paris, the Couvent Saint-Jacques: first arrival
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford chronology gives three years in Paris, 1245-1248. Month unknown, set to the academic autumn. Coordinate corrected to the French Wikipedia point for the Dominican Couvent Saint-Jacques, 48.8472 / 2.3433, at present-day 158 rue Saint-Jacques, rather than the general university-quarter pin used elsewhere in this file.
stops.campa: The order sends him to its own house on the rue Saint-Jacques, from which the Paris Dominicans take their French name, the Jacobins. The convent holds two chairs in the theology faculty and runs a school of its own, and its regent master is Albert of Lauingen, a Swabian who reads everything and who is at this moment paraphrasing the whole Aristotelian corpus into usable Latin. Thomas is twenty. He is heavy, slow to speak, and silent enough among the students that they call him the dumb ox.
suggested_refs: The site of the Couvent Saint-Jacques between today's rue Soufflot and rue Cujas, demolished after the Revolution

stops.name: Cologne, the new studium generale
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford chronology gives 1248 for the move to Cologne under Albert. Month unknown; the order's general chapter met in early summer. Coordinate is the atlas pin for the medieval Cologne studium quarter on the Marzellenstrasse, inherited rather than the city-center point, since a fetch of the Kolner Dominikanerkloster page returned 404.
stops.campa: The general chapter orders a studium generale for the German province and sends Albert to organize it; Thomas goes as his assistant and, in all likelihood, as master of students. Four years in Cologne, taking down Albert's lectures on the Ethics and on Dionysius, doing a secretary's work and learning the method he never afterwards abandons: get the text itself, get it translated accurately, then argue with it. Albert is said to have answered the students' nickname by telling them this ox would bellow so loud the world would hear him.
suggested_refs: Albertus Magnus's paraphrase commentaries on the whole Aristotelian corpus, begun in these years

stops.name: Cologne, ordained priest
stops.date_confidence: R. Only one source consulted names a date and a hand, and it hedges: New Advent says probably in 1250 he was raised to the priesthood by Conrad of Hochstaden. Neither the Stanford nor the Internet Encyclopedia mentions an ordination date or an officiant at all. Read as probably 1250-51, officiant not securely recorded; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Somewhere in the Cologne years he is ordained priest. The only source that supplies a date and a hand is the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, and it says probably 1250 and probably Conrad of Hochstaden, the archbishop then laying out a new cathedral; the modern chronologies decline to give either. So the sacrament behind the Corpus Christi office, the treatise on the Eucharist, and a lifetime of daily Mass is the least documented act in his life. Who laid hands on him, and in what year, nobody now can say.
suggested_refs: Conrad of Hochstaden and the laying of the Cologne cathedral foundation stone, 1248

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: bachelor of the Bible
stops.date_confidence: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy places him back at Paris from 1252; New Advent gives 1251 or 1252. Month set to the autumn term, day defaulted.
stops.campa: Albert sends him back to Paris to begin the theology course, against objections that he is too young for it. A bachelor of the Bible lectures cursorily on scripture, reading the text through without disputing it, and Thomas spends two years at that before he is permitted to argue anything at all. It is the lowest rung of the faculty and he is standing on it at twenty-seven, in a university where his order is resented for holding any chairs whatever. Two sets of those cursory lectures survive from the period, on Isaiah and on Jeremiah.
suggested_refs: The cursory biblical lectures on Isaiah and Jeremiah surviving from this period

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: lecturing on the Sentences
stops.date_confidence: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy places the Sentences lectures inside 1252-1256; no source consulted fixes the years of the individual books. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Every bachelor in Europe lectures on the four books of Peter Lombard, a hundred-year-old anthology of sentences from the fathers arranged by topic. Thomas lectures on them and then writes them out, the Scriptum super libros Sententiarum, running past a million words. It is a young man's book and he will spend the rest of his life rebuilding what is in it. The form he is being drilled in is the quaestio: state the question, marshal the objections, answer them one at a time, and never suppress the strongest one.
suggested_refs: Peter Lombard's four books of Sentences, the standard theology textbook of the medieval West

stops.name: Paris, the university: the war on the mendicants
stops.date_confidence: The Internet and Stanford Encyclopedias both place the mendicant controversy and Contra impugnantes in 1256; month and day unknown. Coordinate is the canonical atlas pin for the University of Paris, inherited from the Llull and Aristotle files, rather than the Saint-Jacques convent point used for the convent stops in this file.
stops.campa: William of Saint-Amour and the secular masters want the friars out of the faculty: men who beg, they argue, have no business holding chairs, and mendicant poverty is a fraud practised on the church. Thomas answers with Contra impugnantes Dei cultum et religionem, written by a man in his early thirties who has not yet been licensed to teach. The quarrel is about two Dominican chairs. It is fought with pamphlets, with sermons, and with appeals to Rome, and it runs for years.
suggested_refs: William of Saint-Amour, De periculis novissimorum temporum, the attack Contra impugnantes answers

stops.name: Paris, the university: received as master of theology
stops.date_confidence: Sources disagree and this is not resolved. The Internet Encyclopedia says he was teaching as Master of Theology in 1256 at thirty-two; the Stanford chronology dates the Dominican chair from 1256; New Advent gives the formal promotion as 23 October 1257. New Advent's precise date is used only to place the stop.
stops.campa: The chancellor licenses him and the faculty receives him, later than it should have, because the secular masters would not admit the friars while the quarrel ran. He takes one of the two Dominican chairs. The office is defined by three verbs, to read, to dispute, to preach, and he will do those three for the rest of his life and hold no other post ever. He is thirty-two. New Advent dates the promotion 23 October 1257; the modern chronologies say 1256, and the disagreement has not been settled.
suggested_refs: The two Dominican chairs of theology at Paris, contested through the 1250s

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: the disputed questions
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford chronology gives the first regency as 1256-1259. The De veritate disputations are conventionally placed inside it; no source consulted fixes the years of individual questions. Month and day defaulted, for ordering only.
stops.campa: A regent master disputes in public on a fixed schedule, and the record of those sessions, cleaned up and written out afterwards, becomes the disputed questions. The objections in them are not straw. He states the case against his own position at full strength, sometimes better than its holders state it, and only then answers it. In the hall any master or bachelor present may attack, and the habit this drills into him is that he does not write a conclusion he has not first heard demolished. Twenty-nine questions survive from the three years, under the title De veritate.
suggested_refs: The Quaestiones disputatae de veritate, twenty-nine questions from the first Paris regency

segments.name: The Italian Decade: Orvieto, Rome, Viterbo

stops.name: Naples, sent home to the Roman province
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford chronology says he was sent back to Italy in 1259; the Internet Encyclopedia places him teaching at Naples 1259-1261. Month set to the autumn term.
stops.campa: Three years is the ordinary term for a regency and his ends on time. The order sends him home to the Roman province, where there is no university and no chair to hold, only the order's own schools. He teaches at Naples for two years. Somewhere in this stretch he begins the Summa contra Gentiles, four books that argue the faith to a reader who grants no scripture, no council, and no authority except reason. It is the one large thing he undertakes with no lecture hall waiting for it, and he will finish it at Orvieto.
suggested_refs: The Summa contra Gentiles, four books, begun in the Italian years

stops.name: Orvieto, lector at the curia of Urban IV
stops.date_confidence: The Internet Encyclopedia places Orvieto 1261-1265; month unknown. Coordinate marks the Orvieto papal quarter and claims no building: the Palazzo Soliano used as a proxy in research is fourteenth-century, built from 1297 under Boniface VIII, and did not exist under Urban IV.
stops.campa: Urban IV keeps his curia at Orvieto, and the order posts Thomas to the Dominican house there as lector, to run its elementary school. The curia next door is where the Greek books and the Greek quarrels are. He finishes the Summa contra Gentiles, compiles the Catena aurea, a gospel commentary stitched entirely out of the fathers, Latin and Greek both, and writes Contra errores Graecorum for a pope trying to negotiate a reunion. His pupils are friars who will preach in Italian market towns and never see a university.
suggested_refs: The Catena aurea, a running gospel commentary assembled wholly from patristic quotation

stops.name: Orvieto, the office of Corpus Christi
stops.date_confidence: Urban IV extended the feast to the Latin church by the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo in 1264, attested. Thomas's authorship of the office has wide scholarly agreement, the BNF 1143 text being placed at or after his Orvieto residence; a papal commission to him personally comes from Tocco's hagiographic life and is tagged R. The August date is the bull's, used to place the stop.
stops.campa: Urban IV extends to the whole Latin church a feast that had been kept only at Liege, and the office for it, the readings and antiphons and hymns of Corpus Christi, is Thomas's. Scholars agree the text is his; the earliest witness is a Paris manuscript, BNF lat. 1143. The man who argues about substance and accident in technical Latin also wrote verses that are sung by people who will never read a page of him. That the pope commissioned the office from him personally comes from the life written for the canonization, and no document of 1264 says it.
suggested_refs: The bull Transiturus de hoc mundo, 1264
BNF lat. 1143, the earliest witness to the Corpus Christi office

stops.name: Anagni, the provincial chapter that sends him to Rome
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the research pool: the documented Anagni connection is the 1265 provincial chapter that assigned him as regent master to Santa Sabina, per the Wikipedia articles 'Anagni' and 'Santa Sabina', not a residence in 1259-61, which no fetched source supports. Month unknown; provincial chapters met in autumn.
stops.campa: The Roman province holds its chapter at Anagni and assigns him to Rome, to open a studium at Santa Sabina. Older biographies put him at Anagni years earlier, in the curia, and the sources consulted here carry nothing for it; what the record does carry is this chapter and this assignment. He is forty. He has taught at Paris, at Cologne, at Naples, and at Orvieto; the house on the Aventine he is now sent to has a handful of friars in it. The acts of the chapter record the assignment and nothing else about him.
suggested_refs: The acts of the Roman provincial chapters of the Order of Preachers, 1265

stops.name: Rome, Santa Sabina: the school and the manual for beginners
stops.date_confidence: The Internet Encyclopedia places the Rome period 1265-1268. Month set to the autumn term; day defaulted.
stops.campa: On the Aventine, in a fifth-century basilica the order had been given by Honorius III, he opens a school for the students of the Roman province and finds the available textbooks useless. Beginners are made to read Lombard's Sentences, ordered by an accident of anthology, or florilegia ordered by nothing at all. So he starts writing his own, a work for beginners arranged as he believes the matter itself is arranged, from God outward and back again. The Summa theologiae is a teaching manual for a provincial school with perhaps a dozen friars in it.
suggested_refs: The prologue to the Summa theologiae, stating its purpose as instruction of beginners

stops.name: Rome, Santa Sabina: the five ways
stops.date_confidence: The Prima Pars is conventionally dated to the Santa Sabina years, c. 1265-1268; no source consulted fixes Question 2 to a year or a month. Date given only to order the segment.
stops.campa: Question two of the first part asks whether God's existence is self-evident, decides that it is not, and then argues it five separate times over from things anyone can see: motion, causation, contingency, degree, and the ordering of things that have no minds. The proofs are not his invention and he never claims they are. The first comes out of Aristotle's physics. The shape of the whole owes a great deal to Maimonides, whom he cites as Rabbi Moyses, arguing the same question for a different scripture eighty years earlier in Cairo.
stops.quote: The existence of God can be proved in five ways.
stops.quote_source: Summa Theologiae, Prima Pars, Q.2 A.3, Respondeo (Dominican Fathers translation, newadvent.org/summa/1002.htm)
sources: Summa Theologiae I, Q.2 A.2-3 (Dominican Fathers translation, New Advent)
suggested_refs: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, whose three-part structure and proofs Thomas works through as Rabbi Moyses
Aristotle, Physics VII-VIII, source of the argument from motion

stops.name: Rome, Santa Sabina: question ninety-two
stops.date_confidence: Question 92 falls in the Prima Pars, written c. 1266-1268 at Santa Sabina; no finer date is available. Citation corrected against the research pool: the 'defective and misbegotten' sentence stands in the reply to the first objection, not in the body of the article.
stops.campa: Question ninety-two asks why woman was made. The answer, given in his own reply and not in a quoted opponent's objection, is that as an individual she is defective and misbegotten, the active force in the male seed having aimed at a likeness of itself and fallen short, and that she was made as a helper to man in the work of generation and in nothing else, since for any other work a man is helped better by another man. He adds in the same reply that with respect to human nature in general she is not misbegotten, being intended by nature for generation. That is the whole of the qualification.
stops.quote: As regards the individual nature, woman is defective and misbegotten, for the active force in the male seed tends to the production of a perfect likeness in the masculine sex.
stops.quote_source: Summa Theologiae, Prima Pars, Q.92 A.1, ad 1 (Dominican Fathers translation, newadvent.org/summa/1092.htm)
sources: Summa Theologiae I, Q.92 A.1, corpus and ad 1 (Dominican Fathers translation, New Advent)
suggested_refs: Aristotle, Generation of Animals II.3, source of the misbegotten-male doctrine Thomas is repeating

stops.name: Viterbo, Moerbeke's Greek and Reginald's hand
stops.date_confidence: The Internet Encyclopedia folds Viterbo into the 1265-1268 Italian period and New Advent lists Viterbo among his posts; month unknown. A coordinated papal translation project commissioned for Thomas is not proven and is not claimed here. Coordinate is the Italian Wikipedia point for the Palazzo dei Papi di Viterbo.
stops.campa: Clement IV's court sits at Viterbo, and among its Dominicans is William of Moerbeke, a Fleming who reads Greek and is putting Aristotle into Latin word for word, straight from the Greek, with no Arabic in between. Thomas uses those versions. Whether he asked for them is not established: older scholarship said he commissioned them and the modern editors will not say it. In these years Reginald of Piperno becomes his socius, the companion who travels with him, hears his confession, and writes at his dictation for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: William of Moerbeke's literal Latin versions of Aristotle, made from the Greek

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: the unrepeatable second term
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford chronology says he was asked in 1268 to return to Paris for an unusual second term as master; other chronologies give the arrival as late 1268 or early 1269. Month set to November; not resolved.
stops.campa: No master returns to a Paris chair twice. The order does it anyway, because Paris is burning in two directions at once. The secular masters have reopened the war on the mendicants, and in the arts faculty a party reading Aristotle through Averroes has arrived at conclusions the theologians will not have. Thomas comes back at forty-three to fight both, and to go on writing the Summa while he fights. The Secunda Pars, the longest thing he ever produced, is written inside this quarrel.
suggested_refs: The Secunda Pars of the Summa theologiae, written during the second regency

stops.name: Paris, the university: against the one intellect
stops.date_confidence: R for the year. The Internet and Stanford Encyclopedias place the polemic in the second regency and the standard critical catalogues date De unitate intellectus to 1270; no month is fixed. Coordinate is the canonical atlas University of Paris pin.
stops.campa: The Averroist thesis is that there is one possible intellect for the whole human race, thinking in each of us and surviving none of us. Thomas answers that this abolishes the thing it was meant to explain: if the intellect is not mine, then it is not I who understand, and the man making the argument has argued himself out of it. He writes against Siger of Brabant, and against a reading of Aristotle he considers plainly a misreading. He ends the book by daring its holders to answer him in public instead of in corners.
suggested_refs: De unitate intellectus contra Averroistas, 1270
Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroists of the Paris arts faculty

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: on the eternity of the world
stops.date_confidence: Standard critical dating within the second Paris regency, 1268-1272, per the Internet Encyclopedia chronology of the period; no month or day is fixed by any source consulted.
stops.campa: Against the murmurers on his own side, he argues that reason cannot demonstrate the world had a beginning in time. That it did begin he holds to be true, because revelation says so, and he holds it to be indemonstrable; a created world with no first moment is not a contradiction. He is telling theologians they have been propping up a doctrine he believes with a proof that does not work. The line he draws here he draws everywhere: what reason can show on one side, what faith holds on the other, and no counterfeiting between them. The book is short and it satisfies nobody.
suggested_refs: De aeternitate mundi contra murmurantes, c. 1271

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: the heretic and the coiner
stops.date_confidence: The Secunda Secundae is written in the second Paris regency, c. 1271-1272; the individual questions are not separately dated in any source consulted. Month set to order the segment.
stops.campa: In the questions on faith he asks whether heretics are to be tolerated and answers that a convicted heretic is to be excommunicated and handed to the secular arm to be put to death, arguing from the death penalty then imposed on counterfeiters: corrupting the faith is graver than corrupting the coin. In the questions on justice he defends the killing of a dangerous man for the common good by the figure of the rotten limb cut off to save the body. Both stand in the body of the article, in his own voice, not in an objection he is about to refute.
stops.quote: Wherefore if forgers of money and other evil-doers are forthwith condemned to death by the secular authority, much more reason is there for heretics, as soon as they are convicted of heresy, to be not only excommunicated but even put to death.
stops.quote_source: Summa Theologiae, Secunda Secundae, Q.11 A.3, Respondeo (Dominican Fathers translation, newadvent.org/summa/3011.htm)
sources: Summa Theologiae II-II, Q.11 A.3 (Dominican Fathers translation, New Advent)
Summa Theologiae II-II, Q.64 A.2 (Dominican Fathers translation, New Advent)
suggested_refs: Summa Theologiae II-II Q.64 A.2, the diseased-limb analogy for capital punishment

stops.name: Naples, San Domenico Maggiore: a school of his own choosing
stops.date_confidence: The Internet Encyclopedia says the Dominicans moved him back to Naples in 1272 and New Advent puts the Third Part there in 1272-73. The provincial chapter at Florence authorizing him to found a studium generale wherever he chose is tagged R; only the year is firm. Month set to the autumn term.
stops.campa: The second regency ends and the Roman province gives him something no master had been given: found a studium generale where you like, on the terms you like. He picks Naples, the city where he took the habit twenty-eight years earlier, and installs the order's new general school in the friary of San Domenico Maggiore. Charles of Anjou's government pays a subsidy for him to teach there. He begins the Tertia Pars, on the Incarnation, and works down toward the sacraments.
suggested_refs: The Dominican studium generale of Naples, founded 1272 under his direction

stops.name: Naples, the Lenten sermons in the vernacular
stops.date_confidence: New Advent situates the final Naples teaching in 1272-73, and the vernacular Lenten cycle is conventionally dated to Lent 1273. Only listeners' reportationes survive, not his own text; day defaulted.
stops.campa: For Lent he preaches to the city in Neapolitan and not in Latin, working through the Creed, the Our Father, the Hail Mary, and the Ten Commandments across the season. The crowds are large enough that listeners take the sermons down as he speaks. He is explaining the first article of the creed to fishermen and dyers in the language they argue in. What survives is those reportationes and not his own copy: the most widely heard thing he ever made exists only as other people's notes.
suggested_refs: The Neapolitan Lenten collationes of 1273, surviving as listeners' reportationes

stops.name: Naples, the chapel of Saint Nicholas: bene scripsisti
stops.date_confidence: R, and deliberately kept separate from 6 December. New Advent and the Wikipedia article both place the crucifix locution in 1273 at Naples, after Thomas finished the treatise on the Eucharist, in the chapel of Saint Nicholas, with no day given. The two episodes are frequently merged and are not the same event. Month set only to order the stop before December.
stops.campa: Brethren find him in the chapel of Saint Nicholas lifted off the floor at prayer, and afterwards the story that runs through the convent is that the crucifix spoke to him: he had written well, what reward did he want. His answer is a single clause, nothing but you, Lord. This belongs to the lives written for the canonization and to no record made that week, and it is not the December episode with which it is habitually confused. The treatise on the Eucharist is finished.
stops.quote: You have written well of me, Thomas; what reward will you have?
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the crucifix at Naples, 1273 (Latin: Bene scripsisti de me, Thoma), with the reply Non nisi te, Domine; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Thomas Aquinas'
suggested_refs: William of Tocco's Ystoria and the canonization depositions, source of the locution

stops.name: Naples, San Domenico Maggiore: the sixth of December
stops.date_confidence: Attested: New Advent says on 6 December 1273 he laid aside his pen and would write no more, and the Stanford chronology quotes the straw remark under the same date. Both state plainly that the nature of the experience, mystical or medical, is unresolved. The straw wording is a widely circulated paraphrase out of the Tocco and Reginald tradition and is tagged R.
stops.campa: He says Mass in the chapel of Saint Nicholas on the feast of its saint and something happens to him at the altar. The sacristan, named in one account as Dominic of Caserta, sees it. Afterwards he does not dictate again. The Summa breaks off at the ninetieth question of the third part, inside the treatise on penance, and stays broken there. Reginald presses him to go on and gets an answer nobody has since explained: everything he has written looks to him now like straw. Whether that was a vision or a stroke, no one then or since can say.
stops.quote: All that I have written seems like straw to me.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Thomas in answer to Reginald of Piperno, December 1273; widely circulated paraphrase from the Dominican biographical tradition, not a verified verbatim text
suggested_refs: The Summa theologiae, Tertia Pars, breaking off at Q.90 on penance
The Supplementum assembled after his death from the Scriptum on the Sentences

segments.name: The Road That Ended in Lazio

stops.name: Naples, setting out for the council
stops.date_confidence: The Internet Encyclopedia says he died on the road to the council. The departure itself is undated in the sources consulted; January 1274 is inferred from a council opening in May and a death on 7 March, and the day is set only to order the stop.
stops.campa: Gregory X summons him to the Second Council of Lyon, called to reunite the Latin and Greek churches, and asks him to bring the Contra errores Graecorum along. He has not dictated a line in seven weeks. He goes anyway, north up the peninsula with Reginald, on the road that would have taken him over the Alps and down the Rhone. He never gets out of Lazio, and the council opens in May without him. He is forty-eight or forty-nine, depending on which birth year is right, and no source consulted gives the day he set out.
suggested_refs: The Second Council of Lyon, opened May 1274 on Latin and Greek reunion

stops.name: Terracina, the fall on the Appian Way
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the research pool: New Advent has him fall near Terracina and then be conducted to Maenza, in sequence, not as a rival tradition, so Terracina and Maenza are not competing accounts. No day is given; month set for ordering. Coordinate corrected to the Wikipedia point for Terracina.
stops.campa: On the Appian Way near Terracina, where the road runs in a narrow strip between the mountain and the sea, he falls. New Advent says only that he fell to the ground; the tradition adds an overhanging branch and a mule. A 2024 paper in a neurosurgical journal builds a chronic subdural haematoma out of that detail and reads the whole last month backward from it, but the paper could not be reached directly for this file and is carried unverified. He is helped up off the road and taken on.
suggested_refs: The 2024 historical-forensic paper in World Neurosurgery proposing a chronic subdural haematoma (PMID 37979685, not verified here)

stops.name: Maenza, the room that belonged to his niece
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the research pool: the Italian Wikipedia article on Maenza says he lodged in the room of his niece Francesca d'Aquino, not a sister, and that the Castello Baronale belonged to the Conti di Ceccano; Torrell likewise makes Maenza the residence of his niece. Day set only to order the stop. The herring story is local tradition, tagged R.
stops.campa: He is carried up to the castle at Maenza, held by the Ceccano counts, where a room belongs to his niece Francesca d'Aquino. The research tradition that made her his sister is simply wrong. He lies in the third-floor rooms some days and will not eat; the household's story, kept locally ever since, is that he asked for fresh herring, that nobody in Lazio could supply such a thing, and that a fishmonger arrived with a load of them. Then he asks to be moved, because a religious ought to die in a religious house.
suggested_refs: The Castello Baronale of Maenza, of the Conti di Ceccano

stops.name: Fossanova, death in a Cistercian house
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia, the Internet Encyclopedia, and New Advent alike: died at the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova on 7 March 1274. Coordinate is the Wikipedia point for Fossanova Abbey, 41.4381 / 13.1958, correcting a pool entry that placed it eight kilometres east.
stops.campa: Three miles from Maenza the Cistercians take him in, at Fossanova, the first house their order founded in Italy. He is said to have come through the gate murmuring a verse of the psalm about a resting place chosen for ever, and to have expounded the Song of Songs to the monks from his bed, though no text of that exposition survives and probably none was ever made. A Dominican dies in a Cistercian house, on the way to a council he was too ill to reach. He dies on the morning of the seventh of March 1274.
stops.quote: This is my rest for ever and ever.
stops.quote_source: Psalm verse reported at his arrival at Fossanova; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Thomas Aquinas'
suggested_refs: Fossanova Abbey, the first Cistercian house in Italy
Dante, Purgatorio XX.67-69, on Charles of Anjou and the death of Thomas

stops.name: Fossanova, the monks keep the body
stops.date_confidence: Burial at Fossanova is attested by New Advent and the Stanford Encyclopedia; the day is set the morning after the death only to order the stop. The boiling of the body to strip the bones is New Advent's account alone and is tagged R.
stops.campa: The Cistercians bury him in their own church. The Dominicans want him back; Fossanova will not give him up, and the argument over where the body belongs runs on for most of a century. The order that owned nothing has produced a member who is now property. Meanwhile the monks do what was done to bodies that might one day have to travel, at least according to the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, which is the only source that says it: they boil the corpse to strip the bones, and keep the bones in the church.
suggested_refs: Medieval mos teutonicus, the boiling of bodies for transport and relic division

stops.name: Paris, the condemnation of two hundred and nineteen articles
stops.date_confidence: Partly R. The 219 propositions and Tempier's censure are attested by the Wikipedia article 'Condemnations of 1277'; the coincidence with the third anniversary of the death, and Kilwardby's Oxford list of thirty theses on 18 March, come from the standard literature and were not re-verified against primary documents here. Thomas is three years dead and was not present; the stop marks an act upon his work, not a journey of his own.
stops.campa: Three years to the day after he dies, the bishop of Paris condemns two hundred and nineteen propositions circulating in the arts faculty, under pain of excommunication. The list names no author. Some of the articles touch positions he held, on individuation and on what God's power can be said to be constrained by. Eleven days later the Dominican archbishop of Canterbury, Robert Kilwardby, prohibits thirty theses at Oxford, one of them the unity of substantial form, which is his. Whether either censure was aimed at him is argued still.
suggested_refs: Etienne Tempier's syllabus of 7 March 1277
Roland Hissette and the scholarship disputing that Kilwardby targeted Thomas

stops.name: Avignon, canonized by John XXII
stops.date_confidence: Attested by New Advent and the Stanford Encyclopedia alike. Thomas had been dead forty-nine years and was of course not present; the stop marks the proceedings about him, after inquiries at Naples in 1319 and at Fossanova in 1321. Coordinate marks the papal site at Avignon; the standing Palais des Papes did not exist in 1323, John XXII living as a guest of the Dominican house there.
stops.campa: The inquiry sits at Naples in 1319 and at Fossanova in 1321, taking depositions from men who had known him and from men who said they had been cured at his tomb. John XXII canonizes him at Avignon on the eighteenth of July, forty-nine years after his death. The friar who lectured to a dozen students on the Aventine is a saint of the universal church. The objection raised in the process was that the miracles were too few, and the answer that came back is the one joke the record preserves: as many miracles as there are articles.
suggested_refs: The canonization inquiries at Naples, 1319, and at Fossanova, 1321

stops.name: Toulouse, the Jacobins receive the bones
stops.date_confidence: Attested by New Advent and the English Wikipedia article alike: 28 January 1369, Urban V's decree dated 1368 and the arrival the following year. The English Wikipedia coordinate for the Church of the Jacobins is 43.6039 / 1.4400; the French Wikipedia convent article's 43.6039 / 1.4403 is used here.
stops.campa: Urban V, a French pope, orders the bones out of Fossanova and into the Dominican church at Toulouse, which he is said to have called the most beautiful of all the houses of the Preaching Friars. They arrive on the twenty-eighth of January 1369, ninety-five years after the Cistercians closed over him, and that day becomes his feast in the calendar. The order that could not pry him out of Cistercian hands now has him in a brick nave in Languedoc. He had never been to Toulouse.
suggested_refs: The Church of the Jacobins, Toulouse, and its 28 January feast

stops.name: Rome, declared Doctor of the Universal Church
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the English Wikipedia article gives 15 April 1567 and the bull Mirabilis Deus. The 1570 Piana edition often cited alongside it was not independently confirmed for this file. Coordinate is a general Rome point; Thomas is nearly three centuries dead and the stop marks an act upon his work.
stops.campa: Pius V, himself a Dominican, declares him Doctor of the Universal Church by the bull Mirabilis Deus, the first of the schoolmen to be named beside the four Latin fathers. Trent has closed four years earlier, and the council's theologians had worked with the Summa open on the table beside the scriptures. By this point the manual he wrote for a dozen friars on the Aventine has displaced Lombard's Sentences as the book on which theology is taught. The bull is dated the fifteenth of April 1567.
suggested_refs: The bull Mirabilis Deus, 15 April 1567

stops.name: Toulouse, Saint-Sernin: the relics after the Revolution
stops.date_confidence: Attested in New Advent: the shrine raised at the Jacobins in 1628 was destroyed in the Revolution, the relics moved to Saint-Sernin, and a gold-and-silver sarcophagus blessed by Cardinal Desprez on 24 July 1878. Coordinate corrected to the Wikipedia point for the Basilica of Saint-Sernin.
stops.campa: The Revolution expels the friars and takes the Jacobins away from the order, and the shrine raised over him in 1628 is destroyed. The relics are carried across town to Saint-Sernin, where the canons keep them for most of a century, until Cardinal Desprez blesses a new sarcophagus of gold and silver over them in July 1878. Competing claims to his skull survive at Toulouse and at Priverno, near Fossanova. Both cannot be true and nobody has adjudicated them.
suggested_refs: The rival skull relic at Santa Maria Assunta, Priverno
The arm relics reported at Naples Cathedral and at Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome, undated in the sources

stops.name: Rome, Aeterni Patris and the Leonine Commission
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the encyclical Aeterni Patris is dated 4 August 1879 in the Vatican text. The encyclical itself does not name the Leonine edition; the Leonine Commission's founding under Leo XIII in 1879 is separately documented and is stated here as a separate fact.
stops.campa: Leo XIII issues Aeterni Patris and instructs the bishops of the world to put Thomas back at the foundation of Catholic teaching, calling him the chief and master of all. What follows is a revival with an institution attached: the Leonine Commission, chartered to produce a critical edition of everything he wrote. Six hundred years after a friar dictated to Reginald in a Naples cell, a papal office is collating manuscripts of those dictated sentences. It began in 1879 and it is still working.
suggested_refs: The Leonine Commission's critical edition of the Opera omnia, begun 1879 and unfinished
Roberto Busa's Index Thomisticus, begun 1946, the machine concordance to the Thomistic corpus

stops.name: Toulouse, the Jacobins again: seven hundred years
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the relics were returned from Saint-Sernin to the Church of the Jacobins in 1974 for the seventh centenary of his death and placed under an altar designed by Yves Boiret. The day is set to his 28 January feast to order the stop; no source consulted gives the exact date.
stops.campa: Seven hundred years after Fossanova the bones come back to the Jacobins and are laid under a plain grey altar in the middle of the nave, designed for them by the architect Yves Boiret. The body has by then travelled further dead than alive: Fossanova, Toulouse, Saint-Sernin, Toulouse again. Fifty years after the altar, Dominicans carry a skull reliquary through fourteen American parishes and thirty or forty thousand people queue to look at it. The reliquary is the property of the Province of Toulouse.
sources: dominicanfriars.org, 'Thousands Flock to Venerate the Skull of St. Thomas'
suggested_refs: The Boiret altar of 1974 in the nave of the Jacobins
The 2024 North American tour of the skull relic, property of the Province of Toulouse
